name: SWE-Gym
description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents. It contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. Tasks are sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories, with pre-configured executable environments and expert-validated test cases. SWE-Gym also includes SWE-Gym Lite (230 instances for rapid prototyping) and SWE-Gym Raw (64,689 instances from 358 repositories without executable environments).
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
publisher: PMLR (Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning)
citeAs: Pan, J., Wang, X., Neubig, G., Jaitly, N., Ji, H., Suhr, A., & Zhang, Y. (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed by identifying Python repositories using SEART GitHub search, extracting task instances from pull requests using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script, versioning instances, and manually configuring executable environments with pre-installed dependencies. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours. Instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure gold patches pass more unit tests than the original code.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Instances that failed environment setup validation were filtered out. Out of 64,689 raw instances from 358 repositories, only 2,438 instances from 11 repositories passed validation and were included in SWE-Gym.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world GitHub issues and pull requests from 11 popular open-source Python repositories. Repositories were selected using SEART GitHub search, filtering for repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors. The raw dataset (SWE-Gym Raw) spans 358 Python repositories with 64,689 instances.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories created before July 1, 2022 were included. No explicit end date for the collection process is stated.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Instances were versioned by associating them with their respective version numbers and setting up environments version-by-version. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. Pre-built Docker images were created for each instance for full reproducibility, totaling 6 TB.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script was used to convert repositories into task instances. Instances were versioned using a generalized SWE-Bench versioning script. Executable environments were manually configured and validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script. Failed instances were filtered out. SWE-Gym Lite was created by following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Executable environments were manually configured by a subset of the authors, requiring approximately 200 human annotation hours. Instances were validated by ensuring the gold patch (human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script. Agent trajectories were labeled as successful or unsuccessful based on unit test outcomes from SWE-Gym.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: OpenHands remote runtime (for parallelizing evaluation and executing unit tests); Docker (for pre-built executable environments)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Trajectory success was determined by unit test pass/fail outcomes. For verifier training, successful and unsuccessful trajectories were balanced by randomly sampling the same number of unsuccessful trajectories as successful ones from each subset. Per-instance capping was introduced to mitigate bias toward easier tasks in the training dataset.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors (researchers from UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, and Apple).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench instance extraction script, SWE-Bench versioning script, SWE-Bench execution-based validation script, SEART GitHub search, SGLang (for verifier inference), torchtune (PyTorch native post-training library), Unsloth (for LoRA fine-tuning)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: SWE-Gym, models, agent trajectories, pre-built Docker images, and training pipeline are publicly released. No explicit versioning schedule or deprecation policy is stated. The dataset is described as a foundation for future research with planned extensions including automatic environment synthesis, additional repositories, task types, and programming languages.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. As agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code. The authors encourage future work to explore frameworks for responsible deployment, including considerations around security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataBiases: The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of total tasks and bokeh representing only one percent. Tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those in SWE-Bench. Repeated sampling shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution biased toward easier tasks. The dataset is limited to Python repositories and does not cover other programming languages.
rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited in environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11 for the main split), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). The dataset covers only 11 repositories out of 358 identified, as manual environment configuration was required. Performance is currently limited by the compute budget for sampling trajectories rather than the number of tasks. Self-improvement results are modest. The dataset may have distribution bias due to inclusion of sophisticated repositories like pandas and MONAI.
rai:dataUseCases: Training software engineering agents (policy models) via rejection sampling fine-tuning and reinforcement learning; training verifier/reward models for inference-time scaling; benchmarking and evaluating SWE agent performance; rapid prototyping with SWE-Gym Lite; future research in automatic dataset synthesis using SWE-Gym Raw.
